title: President's Role in a Parliamentary Democracy
lead: The President of India, as constitutional Head of State under a parliamentary system, occupies a position that is at once ==symbolic and structurally indispensable== — conceived not as a rubber stamp but as a ==constitutional sentinel==.

items.title: Nominal Executive Head
bullets: All Union executive action taken ==in the President's name (Art 77)==
Appoints PM, Ministers, Governors, CAG, ECs, SC/HC judges, UPSC members
Bound by ==‘aid and advice’ (Art 74(1))== — binding post 42nd/44th CAs; ==one reconsideration== permitted

items.title: Legislative Role
bullets: Summons, prorogues, dissolves LS; addresses under ==Art 87==
Assent (==Art 111==): grant, withhold, or return (not Money Bills)
==No fixed timeline== → the ==‘pocket veto’==
Rejection of ==Art 200 reserved state bills== kills the bill

items.title: Ordinance-Making
bullets: Legislation when Parliament isn't in session; approval ==within 6 weeks== of reassembly
Borrowed from the ==GoI Act, 1935==; India, Pakistan, Bangladesh are ==rare global holdouts==

items.title: Judicial — Pardoning
bullets: Pardon, reprieve, respite, remission, commutation — incl. death sentences; ==broader than Art 161==
Exercised on CoM advice; ==limited judicial review== for arbitrariness, mala fides, delay

items.title: Financial Role
bullets: Money Bills need ==prior recommendation (Art 117)==
Budget laid in the President's name (==Art 112==)
==Contingency Fund (Art 267)== at the President's disposal

items.title: Diplomatic & Military
bullets: Treaties negotiated/ratified in the President's name
==Supreme Commander (Art 53(2))== — formal; real decisions with the ==Cabinet Committee on Security==

items.title: Emergency Powers
bullets: The ==most consequential and most contested== dimension
Permits the Union Executive to ==override the federal division of power==

items.title: Discretionary / Reserve Powers
bullets: PM appointment in a ==hung Lok Sabha==, or sudden death/resignation
Dismissing a government that has ==demonstrably lost majority== but won't resign
One-time return of advice (proviso to Art 74(1))
Acting on advice of a ==caretaker Council==

items: ==Ambiguity of ‘aid and advice’ and reserve powers== — no exhaustive definition of genuine discretion; convention rather than codified rule, acute in coalition politics.
==The pocket veto problem== — unlike the US (10-day limit), no deadline; the ==Postal Bill of 1986== was never signed by President Zail Singh.
==Politicisation of hung-verdict choices== (1989, 1996, 1998, 2004) — no codified post-poll alliance protocol.
==Delay on bills and mercy petitions== — decades-long clemency delays raise ==Art 21 ‘death row limbo’== concerns.
==‘Ordinance Raj’== — frequent re-promulgation bypasses scrutiny (Delhi Services Ordinance 2023; repeated Commercial Courts ordinances).
==Misuse of Art 356== — invoked ==~130 times since 1950==, curbed but not eliminated by [[S.R. Bommai (1994)]].
==Erosion of perceived neutrality== — elected by a ruling-coalition-dominated college, often with a prior political career.
==Weak accountability== — Art 61 impeachment so onerous it has ==never been used==.
==Governor–President interface== — bills reserved as a delaying tactic (TN, Kerala, Punjab, WB) drag the office into Centre–state friction.
==No real check on prime ministerial advice== — the 44th CA made reconsideration one-time and non-binding.

items.label: ordinance peaks — 1990s and 1970s, coinciding with political instability
completed impeachment proceedings — Art 61 never successfully invoked
parliamentary democracies retaining ordinance power: India, Pakistan, Bangladesh

head: Country
Head of state model
Reserve/discretionary powers
Distinguishing feature
rows: India
Indirectly elected President; nominal executive
PM appointment in hung Parliament, one-time reconsideration, mercy powers
==Ordinance power retained==; broad Art 356 emergency power
United Kingdom
Hereditary Monarch
Reserve powers by convention — inviting PM, royal assent
==No written constitution== — conventions, not codified rules
Germany
Federal President, elected by Federal Convention
May ==refuse to sign clearly unconstitutional laws==; nominates Chancellor
Strong norm of legal-formal review before signing
Israel
President, elected by the Knesset
Gives mandate to form government to a party leader
==Explicit codified post-election consultation process==
Ireland
President, directly elected
Can ==refer bills to the Supreme Court== for constitutionality (Art 26)
Unique ‘reference’ power — a genuine check absent in India
Italy
President, elected by Parliament + regional delegates
Dissolve Parliament, appoint PM after consultations, refuse unconstitutional decree-laws
Greater use of ==moral suasion== during coalition crises

head: Episode
Significance
rows: ==Zail Singh & the Postal Bill (1986)==
Neither signed nor rejected the Post Office (Amendment) Bill — the classic ==pocket veto==.
==K.R. Narayanan & Bihar President's Rule (1998)==
Returned the Cabinet's Art 356 recommendation — a landmark assertive use of the ==Art 74(1) proviso==.
==A.P.J. Abdul Kalam & Office of Profit Bill (2006)==
Sought reconsideration; bound to sign when returned unchanged — the ==limits of the suspensive veto==.
[[S.R. Bommai (1994)]]
Constrained emergency powers: floor tests, reviewable ‘satisfaction’, no dissolution before parliamentary approval.
[[State of TN v. Governor R.N. Ravi (2025)]]
First-ever assent timelines binding Governor and President — later ==reversed via an Art 143 Presidential Reference==.
==Droupadi Murmu (2022– )==
India's first tribal woman President — a symbolic milestone and a test of ceremonial visibility vs institutional assertiveness.
==Delhi office-of-profit disqualifications (2018)==
President Kovind disqualified ==20 Delhi MLAs== on ECI advice — a quasi-judicial function; later stayed by the Delhi HC.

items: ==Codify timelines== for assent, ordinances and mercy petitions — end the pocket-veto ambiguity
==Post-poll protocol for hung verdicts== — Germany/Israel-style structured consultation + floor test in a fixed period
==Guide emergency powers== — Sarkaria/Punchhi: a reasoned ==speaking order== from the Governor before proclamation
==Introduce a constitutional reference power== — Ireland-style pre-assent advisory reference (distinct from government-initiated Art 143)
==Independent Clemency Review Body== with fixed timelines and transparent criteria
==Transparency in ordinance use== — public urgency justification; cap re-promulgation
==Insulate the office from political career pipelines== — UK Speaker-style visible detachment
==Make inaction reviewable== — extend the mercy-delay logic to bill assent
